newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FEATURE - New wave of refugees would be disaster for Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New wave of refugees would be disaster for Belgrade.

text.p: Aid organisations in Serbia, already over-taxed by 600,000 war refugees, fear a fresh influx of ethnic Serbs when the rebel Croatian enclave of eastern Slavonia reverts to rule by Zagreb soon.
Half the Serb population of eastern Slavonia, up to 60,000 people, could flee to neighbouring Serbia in fear of retribution by returning Croats, aid officials say.
They would place a fresh, and perhaps intolerable, burden on the aid effort at a time when it is struggling to persuade donor countries to continue giving food and other necessities.
"The situation is already critical, an invisible disaster," said Maurice O'Neill of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in Belgrade.

Croatian Serbs seized eastern Slavonia in a 1991 uprising against Zagreb's secession from Yugoslavia. The fighting was scarred by atrocities, including the razing of the town of Vukovar in a Serb siege and the massacre of Croats, including 260 hospital patients.
Elections are being held in eastern Slavonia on April 13 in preparation for the enclave's return to Croatian rule shortly after.

Serb leaders predict half their their people will flee across the Danube river border to Serbia, convinced that Croatian assurances of their safety, made under sustained Western diplomatic pressure, are insincere.
U.N. officials estimate only 15-20 percent will go, mainly those who were involved in atrocities against Croats in 1991.

Many of the Serbs in the enclave have already moved three or four times from other wartorn areas. Their only option now is Serbia, whose economy cannot cope with the 600,000 earlier refugees from the wars in Croatia and Bosnia.
YUGOSLAV ECONOMY IN CRISIS, WIDESPREAD POVERTY
A report commissioned by the IFRC and the Yugoslav Red Cross painted a grim picture of life in postwar Yugoslavia, which comprises only Serbia and Montenegro.
Some 650,000 people are in "severe poverty", with incomes below 50 percent of the poverty line. They include 75,000 who rely solely on soup kitchens for survival.
Almost three million, twice as many as in 1990, are so poor that they cannot satisfy their minimum needs for food.
The life of the refugees is precarious, stricken by poverty, insecurity and the resentment of many Serbian Serbs against the unwelcome guests.
Psychological problems are becoming a major problem in refugee camps, said Branka Panetlic of the Yugoslav Red Cross in Stara Pazova near Belgrade.
"One month ago a mother of two killed herself. Just eight days ago, a son killed his parents and then shot himself, all in just one camp -- Krujesevci. All caused by depression."
The prefabricated camp houses 238 people, 40 of them children, with no electricity or running water. It is wholly dependent on foreign aid for food.
"DONOR FATIGUE" THREATENS AID
But even that lifeline is threatened. International humanitarian organisations say they might soon have to wind up their efforts because of "donor fatigue".
The World Food Programme (WFP) said recently that more than two million people could go hungry in former Yugoslavia this spring unless donors come forward immediately with aid.
Supplies of wheat flour are running out, leaving 2.2 million people short of bread. The WFP called for donations immediately because pledged food takes three months to reach the beneficiaries.
But the European Community Humanitarian Organisation (ECHO) is reducing its Yugoslav operation from feeding 360,000 to 250,000.
"If donor fatigue persists, we might have to cut down our food supplies to feed only emergency cases -- mothers with infants up to 12 months old," O'Neill said.
Yugoslavia's economy has been battered by mismanagement, the disintegration of former Yugoslavia, the wars in Bosnia and Croatia and international sanctions imposed on Belgrade.
Unemployment is officially 25.7 percent, with 800,000 people registered as unemployed. As many workers again are redundant but not registered, the report says.

Annual per capita income was officially $1,500 in 1996, but unofficial assessments put the real figure at $900. The average monthly wage in December 1996 was $163, too little to support a typical family for two weeks.
The death rate, infant mortality rate and under-five mortality rate are all on the rise.
Some 215,000 of the 600,000 refugees in Yugoslavia, which has a population of 10.5 million, are children under 18.

The total cost of food, shelter, health services and education for the refugee population is at least $400 million a year, or 3.4 percent of Yugoslavia's national product, a sum it cannot afford, the IFRC said.
Aid workers see little future for the Serb refugees in Yugoslavia but the faltering peace process holds little hope either of allowing them to return to their old homes in Bosnia or Croatia.
"The only solution is repatriation and for that there is no political will at all," the IFRC's Olga Milanovic said.
